key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset during activity - twisting, pivoting, direct blow, or hyperextension. Common in sports, falls, or accidents. LOCATION: Anterior knee (patellar), medial knee (MCL), lateral knee (LCL), or posterior knee depending on mechanism. DURATION: Immediate pain that may worsen over first 24-48 hours. CHARACTER: SHARP initial pain, then THROBBING and ACHING. May have 'popping' or 'snapping' sound. AGGRAVATING: WEIGHT BEARING, walking, stairs, squatting, knee flexion/extension. RELIEVING: REST, ICE, elevation, NSAIDs. TIMING: Immediate pain, swelling develops over hours, stiffness increases over 24-48 hours. SEVERITY: 5-9/10, severe with activity. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: SWELLING within hours (effusion), BRUISING develops over 24-48 hours, STIFFNESS, difficulty walking or bearing weight, knee may 'give way' or 'lock'. May have audible 'pop' at injury. KEY POSITIVES: Joint effusion, tenderness over affected ligaments, positive Lachman test (ACL), positive valgus/varus stress tests (MCL/LCL), positive McMurray test (meniscus). KEY NEGATIVES: No bony tenderness over patella or tibial plateau (rules out fracture), no obvious deformity.

includes.patient_friendly: all at once or very quickly

red_flags: Inability to bear weight immediately - possible fracture or severe ligament injury
Severe deformity or obvious fracture - obvious knee fracture, call 911
Knee locked in fixed position - possible meniscal tear or loose body, needs urgent evaluation
Severe swelling with severe pain - possible hemarthrosis or severe ligament injury
Numbness or tingling below knee - possible nerve injury or compartment syndrome
